Hacknet is an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC. Dive down a rabbit hoIe as you follow the instructions of a recently deceased hacker, whose death may not have been the accident the media reports. Using old school command prompts and real hacking processes, you’ll solve the mystery with minimal hand-holding and a rich world full of secrets to explore.

Bit, a hacker responsible for creating the most invasive security system on the planet, is dead. When he fails to reconnect to his system for 14 days, his failsafe kicks in, sending instructions in automated emails to a lone user. As that user, it’s up to you to unravel the mystery and ensure that Hacknet-OS doesn't fall into the wrong hands.

Exploring the volatile nature of personal privacy, the prevalence of corporate greed, and the hidden powers of hackers on the internet, Hacknet delivers a true hacking simulation, while offering a support system that allows total beginners get a grasp of the real-world applications and commands found throughout the game.

Fun simulator and manual dexterity game with puzzle elements. You do not have to be a computer-whiz to enjoy Hacknet, but people comfortable at the command-line will enjoy it more. This game takes elements of computer system and makes a fun game out of them. For example, you don't have to know what program runs on the internet port 25, you just have to type that number at the end of the command.

The game simplifies the technical things and makes it fun, while leaving enough to make it also a challenge. It does a great job with the user interface, and I found everything very intuitive. I kept thinking of another hacking simulator, Uplink, and I think Hacknet does a better job with the game interface.

The gameplay was hit and miss for me. I felt like the game is not always consistent with the in-game logic. Find out a password, later it has changed. The commands are not always consistent (like "../filename" does not always work). Some commands are logged on servers but not others, and the purpose of server logs is not made clear. All these are minor issues, because the game is obviously going for fun not realism, but I wish the game did a better job informing me how the game world worked.

Hacknet is best when it feels like an open world, where every bit of information gathered could lead to a new story, when it is used in the right way. Unfortunately, most of the Hacknet stories are trails of breadcrumbs that lead from the email message to a server file, back to a workstation command, and finally a reply message of completion. And these stories can start to feel pretty repetitive, since most of the story time is spent hacking the server defenses, using the same weapon arsenal, each time.

All that said, the stories are well-written, even though most are short, including the primary Bit narrative. The game uses text assets to populate the game world to good effect. And there were just a few opportunities to figure things out independently, which made me feel pretty clever. All said and done, I would recommend this game, especially to computer enthusiasts, with the warning that you will be typing, with some easy timed typing challenges.

Lemme start by saying that this feels like it'd be a pretty niche title.  If the idea of entering commands into a terminal and making notes about IP addresses and passwords does not appeal to you, then turn away now since that's the majority of the gameplay here.


Hacknet fits into the very, very tiny genre of hacking games.  No, not Watch Dogs.  More like Uplink.  And... umm... others?  I honestly don't know of any other titles in this genre, to be honest!  It's a game about breaking into servers, looking for information, and then covering your tracks.  As the game progresses, you'll be tested on your ability to type accurately, multi-task quickly, and ability to dig deep for details in order to progress.  It's a satisfying experience, but I can see where this can get incredibly frustrating, or boring, for some.

Note:  I do not own the DLC and, therefore, it does not factor into this review.

The Good

-Somewhat simulates Real Life™ hacking, versus the "Hollywood" hacking used in Uplink.  It's cool, but I imagine its very simplied and toned down.  But, it's still really neat.

-Makes a fairly daunting premise pretty easy to figure out and play.  The tutorials explain things well enough and stuff isn't thrown at you too fast.  You won't get turned loose on your own until you have a firm grasp of things and you'll never get in over your head.

-Meanwhile, the game is still challenging enough you'll have to stop and think things through at times or get put into situations where the pressure is on and you can't afford to make mistakes.  

-Good music.  It's not great music, persay, but it sets the mood well and isn't distracting.  Not something I'd plan on listening to out of the game, but I definitely appreciate its presence.

-Workshop support is always a good thing to have in a game.  I've not tried the stuff out yet, but it seems like people can do things like add new missions and stuff, which is cool and can add a lot of longevity to the game.


The Neutral

-The plot...  its serviceable, but a bit predictable.  Kinda a shrug rating.


The Bad

-The cost might be one of them.  The game isn't very long and, combined with the next point, might make $10 a little steep.  Granted, there's incredibly few games in this sort of genre and mod support will help shore up the major short coming.

-The big, big, big point though, is the game is short and fairly linear and, therefore, has low replay value.  There's secrets to explore and discover and some parts of the game are procedurally generated, making for a somewhat different experience each time.  However, it lacks the open nature of Uplink, its progression systems, or two options of storylines.  Tools are given when you needed them, no sooner and no later.  Side unlock stuff are mostly cosmetic things, like new themes.  There's very few side missions and you'll have to do most of them to progress either way.  You're looking at 5-6 hours for a single play through and it'll feel like it's over just a little bit too soon.  This is no doubt the biggest thing to consider when thinking about buying this game.  Although, remember, Workshop support can potentially alleviate this issue.

-The server map gets rather unwieldly late game, as its hard to tell which server is which or select the right one.  Some sort of filtering tool would have been a huge help here, especially since most servers only get used once or twice and then never again.


All in all, this is a tough recommendation.  It's a fairly niche title and you may wish to wait for a sale to pick it up.  But there's very, very few experiences on the market that are anything like it, so it's definitely worth giving a shot if only for novelty's sake.

Received free from HumbleBundle promotional offer.

Gameplay: Good (4/5)
The command-line-style navigation and execution takes some getting used to at first, but it's pretty cool once you get into a groove.  The process of hacking each new target also leaves you feeling like a HackerMan™, though the process doesn't change too much and gets a little repetetive near the end.  Still, the progression is well done and finding each new program is like uncovering a lump of gold.

Ambience: Excellent (5/5)
Honestly, for a hacking game HackNet knocks it out of the park.  The music is fantastic, and the UI and color schemes fit right in there with it.  Despite being singleplayer, every aspect of the game feels like you're connected to the world wide web and part of a bigger picture, so that's a five there too.

State of the Game: Good (4/5)
I didn't encounter any bugs during my time playing, and consistenly got over a hundred frames.  The only nitpick I have is that some of the triggers for each mission might not be as intuitive as they should be, and once or twice I had to look up exactly what I needed to do to move forward.

Story: Good (4/5)
While nothing outstanding, HackNet's story is good and I did feel an emotional pull at some points.  It isn't always in your face - on some occasions, it takes the backseat and lets you run off and do other jobs - but when it is the main focus, it does a good job.  It clocks in at around 8 hours, although there are plenty of community extensions if you want more.

Verdict: solid yes!  I'd consider it worth full price ($10), but it seems to go on sale frequently and with a sizable discount so don't let the price tag dissuade you.

It is the first hacking game I played, and I had no idea it would be this fun.

The hacking aspect in the game is fairly simple. You don't have any programming to do. You just use some basic unix-like commands and are given some cracking tools (programs) to hack into various systems with an ip address. It can become a bit repetitive at some point. But the main fun in the game is the investigative work you have to do to reach the goal of your missions. What tools should I use, where should I hack next, how to find the password I need...

Also, there are tons of text files (IRC, docx...) everywhere, filled with silly dialogues, dumb jokes, parodies... Most have strictly nothing to do with the completion of the game, but some of the files content is simply hilarious...

Anyway, if you like puzzle games, enjoy reading and have a good sense of humor, I definitely recommend this game to you!
